Text | Fanyu Meng

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Some well-known breakfast cereals have a sound all their own when you pour on the milk. The most famous of all is Rice Krispies’ “Snap, Crackle, Pop.”

I looked it up and discovered, to my surprise, that these three words are also the names of the higher-order time derivatives of displacement: the fourth, fifth and sixth.

When cereal is toasted, tiny cavities form inside it. As it soaks up the milk, the walls of these cavities rupture, producing the “snap.” Matelys, a research lab in France, has developed software that simulates the sound of cereal, which can be used to check food quality and shelf life.

Before turning to the sound of cereal, Matelys studied the acoustics of other foods, to see whether useful information could be extracted from acoustic signals at all.

Take bread. If you leave a slice out for a few days, how does its sound absorption coefficient change? Bread, it turns out, is a naturally gifted porous material, and a rather fine one. The sound absorption coefficient is the physical quantity that describes how well a material absorbs sound energy at a given frequency; the higher it is, the more absorbent the material. The figure below shows, for two different breads left out for eight days, how the absorption coefficient below 2,000 Hz changed from day to day. The absorption coefficient shifts over time, and the overall trend is upward. As the days pass, the bread loses moisture and hardens, which changes its structure and, in turn, its acoustic behavior. Both breads show the same thing: the longer they sit, the more sound they absorb overall.

So what good is that? If the bread has no bag, so you can’t see the best-before date, and there’s no mold on the surface, you can still tell how long it has been sitting out from its absorption coefficient!

Back to cereal. Matelys simulated its sound absorption and got results that agreed well with the measurements. As you can see, cereal absorbs sound very much like a porous composite material. The simulation relies mainly on three parameters:

Porosity: how much free space there is inside the cereal

Airflow resistivity: how much resistance the cereal offers to air passing through it

Tortuosity: how “twisted” the pore channels in the cereal are

The green curve in the figure is the result of the simulation with all the pore channels removed. The cereal absorbs less sound, which means the famous “crackle” would vanish along with them!

Cereal makers can compare their products against the simulation results to see whether something has gone wrong with quality. Other food companies can put acoustics to work too, for quality control of food or food packaging. When you open a yogurt pot, for instance, the pot’s absorption coefficient changes with how far the lid is open. Notably, when the lid is fully closed, the absorption coefficient shows a pronounced peak at around 500 Hz, a feature that could well be used to check the quality of yogurt packaging.

In fact, when it comes to quality control, acoustics is hardly an untested weapon; it just looks rather new in the food industry. It is already widely used in end-of-line (EOL) quality control, for example. In the automotive industry, parts have to pass quality checks before they leave the production line. There are plenty of traditional methods, of course, such as visual inspection and temperature and dimensional measurements, but acoustic testing is contactless, fast and cheap, and combined with machine learning it is bound to go far. Beyond traditional manufacturing, any industry that involves quality inspection could give it a try. With timber, for example, you can tap the wood and measure its acoustic response to judge its quality. The possibilities go on: the sky’s the limit!

Reference: altair.com
